* That this House condemns the Government for imposing punitive tax measures; high energy and interest costs; and general economic uncertainty upon the mining sector, all of which have led to the loss of jobs in Canada and a loss of foreign markets and foreign exchange, and urges that a special committee of this House be struck to investigate and recommend immediate solutions to the problems facing the mining industry in Canada and the economic hardship and despair imposed upon thousands of Canadians in mining communities from coast to coast.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if this motion before the House today is adopted, we would see the creation of a special parliamentary committee to examine the very serious structural problems facing the Canadian mining industry today.
Naturally, the current slump in Canada's mineral production can be linked to a large extent with the world-wide economic recession. But many of the problems confronting our mines and their employees started over a decade ago and are unrelated to the recession. It is only during the past 18 months that this decline and the importance of this industry to Canada has become to visibly apparent to all Canadians because of the consequent widespread unemployment in the mining industry.
The result has been the hardship, the suffering, the uncertainty felt in mining communities across Canada, and the closing down of many company towns. These troubles began with the closing of Uranium City operations in northern Saskatchewan in December of 1981. Over subsequent months we have witnessed the decline of the potash industry in Saskatchewan, the asbestos industry in Quebec, iron ore in Quebec and northern Ontario, the closing of the major nickel mining and smelting operations in Sudbury for an extended period of time, the decline of our copper and molybdenum industries and, most recently and regrettably, the decline of our coal markets in Pacific Rim nations. This all translates into considerable human suffering and loss of income.
[DOT]	(1110)
I want to say at the beginning that stop-gap measures will not be enough to solve these problems. The use of Section 38 under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the concept of work sharing and even programs like ILAP will only be useful if
they lead to a meaningful investment in future plant and opportunity to produce and to market more competitively those bountiful mineral resources which we have throughout Canada.
These kinds of stop-gap measures, which I am sure the Minister will be speaking of in her rebuttal, will not affect more than a small number of those thousands and thousands of Canadian mine workers who are presently unemployed. They will be of little value unless they are geared to certain long-range goals which are established by the Government of Canada in consultation with the mining industry.
A special parliamentary committee, as provided for under the new House rules, would be the best way to tackle this issue. It would deal with the issue openly and could act with the urgency needed as a consequence of years of neglect, not only by the federal Government but by provincial Governments, in coming to grips with these very serious problems.
In Canada we have a great untapped potential in bountiful mineral reserves. It is inexcusable for the Parliament of Canada to overlook this important sector of our economy and the contribution that that mineral wealth can make to the wellbeing of all Canadians. And it is obvious that policy papers prepared by the bureaucracy are not the way to go towards solving this problem.
It has now been a year and two months since the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) released her ill-fated policy paper, which at the time was called a discussion paper on mineral policy, yet nothing has come of that paper that we have been able to detect. In spite of a great and costly work effort by hundreds of officials in the Minister's Department, the policy paper missed the mark in terms of the real issues of priority that should have been addressed. It is not surprising that this paper drew harsh criticism from every quarter. However, the concern created by the proposed mineral policy resulted in a number of thoughtful and detailed responses. It would be tragic if these responses were ignored by the Minister as she puts her embarrassment under the rug, so to speak, with respect to this policy paper.
It is time that the Minister, the Government and her Department began listening to the real and long-range needs of the industry. There is a chronic need for a whole new approach to rejuvenating our mining industry. A parliamentary committee could map out the ground rules and objectives in this regard that should be followed by all Government departments, both at the federal and provincial levels. This would go a long way toward establishing the security and confidence that is essential to the growth of mining in Canada.

For example, some of the issues which such a committee would address might fall into the following categories. Such a committee should look at the elements of production costs such as wages, the impact of labour relations on those wages, the costs of energy, the costs of capital, in particular the interest rates available to Canadian investors and industry in comparison with those interest rates available in other parts of the world, the burden of taxation and the royalties. All of these elements of production costs should be compared with our other major world competitors to find out, for example, why it is that they can put nickel on the market at a dollar a pound cheaper than the Canadian producer can market it.
We must look at the question of efficiency of production. Canada's mining industry prides itself in being on the leading edge of modern technology. However, are we keeping abreast of the new and emerging developments that are being exploited in new mines being opened up around the world? On the question of economies of scale, can we justify a lot of small, marginal mines or should we be looking to larger scale activities? How does that question of scale relate to practices in other countries? What about marginal deposits and the important costs of infrastructure such as hydro-electric power and transportation?
These matters must be addressed and put into the context of what our chief competitors are doing in the Iron Curtain countries, such as the Soviet Union, in Australia and in Third World nations which are increasingly eroding our share of world markets. We must find out why it is that the Canadian mining industry of recent times has not been able to attract sufficient investment capital. We must think about world marketing strategies and the potential for growth in the Canadian mining industry. My colleagues and I this morning, and later today, will deal with many of these subjects in detail in order to provide the catalyst and framework in which a parliamentary committee could take a detailed and, I believe, very helpful look at this serious problem.
Surely, an industry which accounts for almost 10 per cent of our Gross National Product deserves better than it has been receiving at the hands of this Government. Eighty per cent of our mineral production is diverted to export which makes a very important contribution to our balance of payments and our Gross National Product. Therefore we must not merely pick away at the problem in a piecemeal fashion, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that will not be the practice of Liberal Members opposite. We must look at this problem in a very constructive and long-range way in order to restore that tremendous potential which had been developed over many years in the North and in the far-flung regions of Canada which created that important pool of wealth for the benefit of all Canadians.
The impact of mining, Mr. Speaker, is felt in every region of our country. It accounts for 4.1 per cent of all capital and repair expenditures and one-fifth of all our national exports. It normally employs 135,000 workers, and 10 per cent of our total labour force through indirect employment, with a multiplier of some five-fold over the actual number of people working
in mines and smelters. The mining industry makes up 60 per cent of all railway freight which is handled in our country.
Total metal and mineral production in 1981-82 was over $31 billion, but in 1982 there was a substantial loss. There was a 20 per cent decline in the value of our mineral production largely going to export with consequent multimillion dollar losses, both for the major mining industries of Canada and the Treasury of Canada; because with major losses being declared, the flow of tax revenue to Government has been heavily depleted in the past fiscal year.
In the policy paper called "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s", which accompanied the 1981 budget, the Government actually identified the importance of the mining industry and said that one of its leading economic priorities, to quote from that document, "lies in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources". The quote continues;
To back this up, the Government is allocating over $60 billion to economic development expenditures in the period to 1981-86.
That was a year and a half ago, Mr. Speaker, and as yet, other than some make-work help-out programs, we have seen little action in getting on with the important job of developing a greater opportunity for Canada's mineral industries around the world. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in fact it has not merely been a matter of passiveness. Certain federal policies have amounted to a virtual attack on Canada's mining industry. This Government has indulged in destructive tax policies and interventionist adventures which have seriously eroded the investment climate for this resource sector in general. Thousands of jobs have been lost as these Government actions brought a curtailment of mineral development during the 1970s. It is a particularly upsetting situation for those who recognize the potential of the industry and the contributions it has made to Canada's past prosperity.
Mining established a foothold and flourished in Canada during the post-war period, Mr. Speaker, thanks to federal tax policies which encouraged resource exploration and development; but these policies were abandoned in the late 1960s and the industry came into a period of decline. The major step down the road to the present insanity was a decision to scrap the tax-free period, the three-year front end tax-free period, for new mines. This tax policy, or to call it by its more correct term, "tax deferral", allowed mining companies to be tax free for the first three years of developing a new mining project, with the understanding that that inducement would be repaid to Government, or there would be some recognition by way of profit sharing which would be extended to the Government after the mine had been developed. That program allowed the elimination of front-end loading on struggling marginal industries which were trying to raise capital and finance major new capital investment.
My hon. and eminent colleague, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), will talk in
May 9, 1983

greater detail later about how this tax policy was introduced and how effective it was, and then how over a period of time, because of various attempts by various provincial Governments and the federal Government to grab more of the revenues from these resources, the benefit of this particular measure was lost. It has been replaced by heavy front-end taxation which provides a tremendous disincentitve to getting on with the development of new mining projects at a world competitive price structure.
Destructive taxation, Mr. Speaker, has had a dramatic effect beause it not only took money away from struggling mineral operations but also created an unstable and unfriendly investment climate for an industry which requires long-term planning. The harm done by federal policy was unfortunately often magnified by provincial Governments, such as the shortlived experiment with socialism in British Columbia. There are a lot of British Columbians who are, since Friday, thanking their lucky stars that that Party did not take hold of Government again in British Columbia. We were able to witness on Friday morning the resurgence in trading even on the Toronto Stock Exchange in mining stocks which have been on hold for six months because of the concern that an NDP Government might have been re-elected in that Province last week. The British Columbia mine workers and mine companies are, of course, still recovering from the royalty on mineral production which was in effect under the NDP Government from 1972 to 1975. That short period alone chased thousands of jobs and millions of investment dollars out of British Columbia.
Similarly, the private sector potash industry in Saskatchewan was brought to its knees by the absurd levels of taxation introduced by the NDP regime in that Province. While the federal Government cannot be blamed therefore for all of the misdeeds of its provincial counterparts, it must also be held partially accountable for the absence of any meaningful progress on federal-provincial agreements on mining taxation during the 1970s. Such an agreement could have spared miners and mining companies and Canadians generally the insanity of taxes being compounded on taxes and payments to the various levels of Government which approached 100 per cent of profits, and more in many cases. This was certainly the case for certain operations in Saskatchewan under the Bla-keney Government.
Aside from trying to co-ordinate mineral policy with the Provinces, Mr. Speaker, the federal Government should get its own act together. Although the work of M and R scientists is often laudable, the Department of Finance and other Government agencies have been hostile to mining. This has never been so evident as it was in the case of the two MacEachen budgets in November, 1981 and June, 1982. To quote one unnamed spokesman for the mining industry, "after the two MacEachen disasters anything would be welcome, but it is interesting that now they screwed it up, they are giving the economy back to business saying: 'Fix it up' ",
That is a characteristic, Mr. Speaker, of the budget which was introduced on April 19, which did take certain positive measures, as I am sure the Minister will be proclaiming in a few moments, which are designed to assist the mining industry.

But there is no comment on the damage that was done by previous budgets with the reduction in the capital cost allowance, the non-deductibility of soft costs, the question of taxation of interest costs, tax on work in progress, and the tax audits being conducted vigorously against insider traders in mining companies and the general anti-investment thrust of previous Government policies.
It is commendable, Mr. Speaker, that in the budget of April 19 a decision was made to make the 33 1/3 per cent mining depletion allowance deductible against non-resource income for investors in the junior mining exploration companies. This is a welcome move, long overdue, but the benefits of the decision will be seriously undermined by the continuing unfair tax treatment of employees, officers and directors of junior mining companies, as I have already pointed out, where Revenue Canada is trying to tax as income the return on investment which was earned by consultants and professionals in exchange for their participation in junior mining companies. This sort of measure, which will be outlined further by one of my colleagues later today, has had a tremendous negative impact on the availability of investment capital to the mining industry.
The other matter the Minister will probably refer to relates to some changes in the investment tax credit and other initiatives contained in the April 19 budget. These are designed to provide an incentive to finance major capital projects in the mining sector. The only problem is that the industry is presently in a state of over capacity. Until we find a way to market our products more competitively internationally, no amount of additional investment capital will be able to deal with the long-range problem.
The most contentious of the initiatives of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in recent years is the plan to tax the housing and travel benefits traditionally received tax-free by workers in the North and other remote areas. This tax will add significantly to the cost of mining in northern Canada for both companies and, ultimately, employees. The decision last December to phase in the new taxes did nothing but reaffirm the industry's view that the Government is determined to destroy and weaken Canadian mining, particularly in the areas of Canada where new exploration and development are essential.
The assumption of the Minister of Finance that mine unions can negotiate contracts to make up for these lost benefits borders on the ridiculous. These unions are negotiating with companies which have been recording massive losses and which have often shut down their operations for extended periods, which is hardly an atmosphere for taxing increased benefits.
There are roughly 35,000 miners still off the job in Canada today, almost 30 per cent of the mining work force, despite the resumption of work in Sudbury and the promise of developments in the Hemlo gold field. The threat of the northern

May 9, 1983
Supply
benefits tax remains as a major obstacle to the return to work for many of these workers.
The Minister of Finance and his colleagues have asserted that this tax will put northerners on an equal footing with other Canadians, but this ignores the reality that these benefits are essential to making life in the North comparable to that elsewhere. The tax also ignores the many long-term decisions which have been made by individuals and companies in the belief that this provision would not be changed.
As I mentioned before, a stable investment climate must be a major priority in order that the mining industry may prosper. However, instability has been the policy of the Government, not only through destructive tax policies, but also with its stand on foreign investment and Government involvement in the economy. The Foreign Investment Review Agency, which has influenced the ownership of operations such as the Cyprus Anvil mine in Faro, Yukon, remains a major concern to investors despite the Government's decision to back off on FIRA during the recession.
FIRA's unsettling effects in the investment community are augmented by the newly formed Canada Development Investment Corporation which hangs like a sword of Damocles over the heads of everyone in the private sector. The mining industry is acutely aware of the threat posed by this super holding company because of CDIC's 1980 takeover of the Kidd Creek mine near Timmins, Ontario. This little adventure, tied to the National Energy Program, resulted in $400 million in new debt being created and imposed on the once profitable mine.
Petro-Canada's expansionary activities can only be viewed with alarm by the mining industry, especially since Petro-Canada's involvement in coal production in northeastern British Columbia demonstrates its ability to become involved in the mining sector. Now the new Chairman of the Board of Westcoast Transmission, who happens to be the President of Petro-Canada, indicates that he is prepared to move in, take control of British Columbia's natural gas industry and intrude into other sectors of the economy as well.
Last year's purchase of BP interests show us that the Government has no intention of repairing the damage it has done to investor confidence over the years. These and other Government policies have had a staggering impact. As I pointed out at the beginning of my speech, in the late '60s, the start of the Trudeau years, we saw a move toward the harmful tax policies of today.
We have before us a rather bleak situation and much opportunity to improve upon it. We in this Party are suggesting today that a special committee of the House be initiated immediately and be mandated to travel the country to consult with industry and Government Departments at both federal and provincial levels. We need to come up with some constructive proposals for dealing with this serious problem as to why Canada is declining so miserably in its pursuit of competitive opportunities around the world.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member made reference to the three-year tax holiday. We know why that was done; it was in the interests of increasing the development of mines. The information I have is to the effect that so much high-grading was being done that it was not really in the longterm interests of the employees or of the mines that all of the high grade ore be taken out in the first three years during the tax holiday. They would then find themselves in difficulty down the road. Is this not in fact what occurred?

I think the situation is exactly opposite to what the Hon. member describes. The elimination of this tax holiday made it much less attractive to develop marginal or low-grade deposits. Therefore the emphasis in investment was directed even more strongly toward the development and exploitation of high-grade deposits. That ensured that we missed out on the opportunity to develop a lot of new low-grade deposits. As the record will show, it has been much more difficult to finance through investment those low-grade deposits until perhaps the initiatives of the budget of April 19.
I think the most important thing we must recognize is that if we do not make it attractive for investors to invest their cash when they know they will not make a return for at least three to five years on exploration and development of a new mine, then we will just not continue to expand the number of competitive sources which have a profound influence on Canada's ability to compete internationally in the sale of minerals.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member can have it both ways. In one breath he is telling us that it had a detrimental effect on the low-grade ore because miners were moving to the high-grade. I suggest, with respect, that the high-grade mines will operate whether there is a tax holiday there or not. The area we should be working on is the low-grade. These mines will not operate and will not be in place, but maybe encouragement of these low-grade deposits is not in the long-term interest of the employers. We might have been encouraging miners or people who were doing this kind of investing to get into the low-grade aspects for the three-year tax holiday time, have these miners working for that time frame, and then being unable to work after the tax-free holiday.

Mr. Speaker, I think the point is that as we expand our capacity to produce minerals, whether from high-grade or low-grade deposits, those developments will become profitable. Even granted the three-year tax holiday, there would be an implied contractual commitment that the benefit of that tax holiday would be paid back once profits were earned. It is ludicrous to suggest taxing paper profits. If the Hon. Member is suggesting that we allow only the high-grade deposits to proceed by denying the three-year tax benefit, which would essentially encourage competitive sources of production, then I cannot agree with him, Mr. Speaker. The whole purpose of the unloading of the front end of the tremendous investment burden that mining investors face is to get
May 9, 1983

more capital into mining and to stop this nonsensical situation of taxing income before it is ever really earned.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member draws certain conclusions from British Columbia. In one instance he spoke about Saskatchewan, and in another instance he spoke about NDP Governments being somehow or other to blame for the downturn in the mining industry. There are two questions I have for the Hon. Member. How does he explain the difficulties the mining industry has in the Province of Ontario, where the NDP has never been the Government?
And never will be.

Well, who knows about that? That is not a big problem, frankly. Second, the Hon. Member speaks about the need to create a good climate in which investors can invest their money. What does he think of the climate in Chile, Argentina, Guatemala or Indonesia where these same investors are investing who invest in Canada? They have to go there and deal with people who stand with a gun at their head in order to make deals. They do not seem to be withdrawing with the possible exception of Guatemala. They do not seem to be finding any difficulty dealing there. Does the Hon. Member really think that anyone believes his unadulterated crap?
Order!
Back to the fire department.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) belies a great unease when he has to finish his question with an arrogant adjective such as that. I would not mind if the Hon. Member would allow me to answer the questions he has put.
In the case of the Province of Ontario I think it is fair to say that many people in the mining community are not terribly pleased with the excessive bureaucracy that has to do with the trading in shares of mining stocks on the Toronto Stock Exchange compared to the situation, I might add, on the Vancouver Stock Exchange which has experienced record trading in these areas in recent months. That is not to say you can draw any valid parallels between the state of affairs in the Provinces of Saskatchewan or British Columbia under NDP Governments-and I might add Manitoba-and the situation in Ontario. I do not see the Ontario Government putting aside massive reserves of land, establishing Crown corporations to mine the minerals of Ontario in the name of the Crown and establishing a cartel and participating in a cartel in the marketing of those minerals, as was the case with the Province of Saskatchewan. I do not see the Province of Ontario driving out investment capital from the mining industry. In fact, if you look at the situation in Hemlo in the gold fields in the Timmins area, Mr. Speaker, you will see a tremendous amount of enthusiasm and excitement over the development of new mining ventures there.
I do not think it is fair to suggest that the Conservative Government of Ontario is practising in any way the types of

socialist or interventionist measures that have become commonplace with NDP provincial Governments in western Canada.
If other Members would like to ask additional questions I will sit down, but I have one other question to answer which the Hon. Member asked me. It had to do with the situation in other parts of the world. I agree that it would be desirable for Canadian mining companies to keep their investment dollars in Canada, to enjoy a fair return on those investments and keep the jobs in Canada if our taxation and royalty structures and the predictability of Government regulations were such that they would. It is interesting that companies have been induced to take their investment elsewhere because of the negative policies of federal and provincial Governments with regard to the mining industry.
It is even more appalling to learn, as we did last week, that the Canadian Government is heavily engaged in financing mining ventures in many of these countries through the Canadian Export Development Corporation, CIDA, and other initiatives. I would like to know what my NDP friends think about the following example. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) announced on May 4, 1983 that the Canadian Government would be heavily assisting the development of a major new coal mine in Indonesia. He was present in Jakarta for the signing of the contract under which Canadian companies would get some spin-off work in relation to developing this coal mining project in South Sumatra.
The interesting facet of this story is that there is a policy which the Indonesian Government implements that says it cannot accept any investment in a venture of this sort unless there is an equal amount of money spent on contracts with the Indonesian Government in relation to any benefits that are taken out of the country. I think the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is well aware of that. Here we have the Canadian Government setting up a new coal mine in South Sumatra which will produce by 1985 nine million tonnes of coal a year, which is equivalent to the entire production of the northeast coal field in British Columbia. The Indonesian Government says: "We welcome your assistance and the involvement of your mining companies but the condition is that you have to allow us to win Government contracts to import Indonesian goods to Canada", equal to the value of the investment we are making there. That seems rather ludicrous, Mr. Speaker, because there is no net gain for Canada. In fact, there is a net loss for Canada. We are adding another nine million tonnes a year production capacity in another country and the Canadian Government is aiding and abetting the loss of Canadian jobs in the process.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and take part today in the debate on the motion that in part urges a special committee of this House be struck to investigate and recommend immediate solutions to the problems facing the mining industry and the workers in Canada. I think we should go beyond that to the communities involved in the Canadian mining industry because they are the ones most affected by the decisions being made.
I would like to refer to some of the happenings in my riding of Kootenay East-Revelstoke regarding decisions of the Government of Canada. The Minister is well aware of these matters as I have approached her in that regard. First I refer to a statement made by Senator Olson on August 6, 1980 respecting the development of northeast coal. In part he said:
We recognized that federal financial assistance to facilitate the development of northeast coal was a sound investment for Canadians as long as our contribution reflected a responsible and reasonable level of potentially recoverable costs on the project. The current proposal from British Columbia, however, provides no indication that either Government could directly recover its investment.
Development of the northeast British Columbia coal resource would of course be of great advantage to the buyers... since it would diversify their sources and provide security of supply. Quite plainly, the coal-buying interests must be prepared to pay a higher price per tonne if they are to benefit from accelerated development of this Canadian resource.
Also Senator Olson pointed out that there were already large quantities of marketable high-grade metallurgical coal available from British Columbian Albertan mines for shipment to Japan at prevailing world prices. Then in April, 1981 an agreement was struck between British Columbia and the federal Government. At that time Senator Bud Olson said:
I am here on behalf of Prime Minister Trudeau and the Government of Canada to congratulate the Canadian and Japanese companies on their
successful negotiation of the largest export agreements ever achieved between our two countries. I endorse Mr. Nemoto's remarks both now and during the negotiations of the importance of these agreements to the healthy and growing trade relationship between Canada and Japan.
It has been an honour for me to lead the federal Government's involvement in this project. I had the constant encouragement and support of the Minister of Transport, ... who, while he cannot be here today, has ensured the full cooperation of the National Harbours Board and the Canadian National Railways.
These are the kinds of changes the Government has made, without consulting the communities or the coal industries involved, that have created tremendous hardship. Since that time, 2,000 coal workers in my riding have been faced with a six-week lay-off. Also they were notified of another pending four-week lay-off. They are supplying the same markets which the northeast will supply. Not only is the Minister and the Government contributing almost $1 billion in infrastructure for northeast coal, but they will devastate the supply of southeast coal.
They have also appointed a marketing agency headed by a former Minister of the House, Ron Basford, at $800 per day and with a full-time office in Vancouver which will be in charge of the marketing of coal from the northeast. On the board of directors of that marketing board will be a Minister of the Province of British Columbia, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), his Deputy Minister, the head of British Columbia Hydro, the head of CN Railways and representatives from the new community of Tumbler Ridge.
This structure is being put in place to ensure the marketing of northeast coal. How does the Minister expect southeast coal to compete in the same markets with that structure in Vancouver to carry out discussions with foreign buyers? This is a very serious matter. I think the Government and the task force for which the Conservative Party is calling can do some good for the communities concerned. As the mining critic for the New Democratic Party, I support the idea of a committee travelling across the country and the inclusion of input from the people and communities involved.
At this point I would like to speak about the Iron Ore Company of Canada in Schefferville which has created a very serious problem for thousands of its laid off workers. As we know, Brian Mulroney is the head of the company. It has offered its workers 50 per cent of their costs to leave the area.
A generous offer.

It may sound like a generous offer but, as the Conservatives know, the only way out of Schefferville is by travelling on the railway of the Iron Ore Company. It will receive back the very funding it gave the workers, and in fact is asking the federal Government to come in and make up any difference. We have a responsibility to these communities and workers, but the company officials have an even greater responsibility than just turning their backs and saying that they have investments in South America, South Africa and Guatemala and that they are supplying their markets from those areas.
May 9, 1983

The Hon. Member was quite correct when he mentioned that the federal Government was spending moneys in other countries. Our Party brought that very fact before the House and questioned the Government as to why these development moneys were being spent in other countries, particularly at a time when there were problems in our mining industries.
I want to discuss another matter with regard to coal. Approximately 13 million to 14 million tonnes of coal are shipped to Japan from the Kootenays each year. Four mining companies are involved in the shipment. It is a very important commodity for the coal fields in my riding. Because there have been such discussions, I know that the Government is aware that Ontario Hydro purchases in the neighbourhood of 14 million tonnes of coal a year from the Americans; 14 million tonnes of coal come from the United States to Canada for Ontario Hydro. I want to emphasize very clearly that the amount of toxins coming from American coal is seven times greater than that from Canadian coal. We in the House talk about acid rain, and I want to say to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) that it is time that we started to look at what is happening right here in Canada.
The Conservative Party has criticized the mining policies of the New Democratic Party in British Columbia. The Conservative Party may have had just cause to complain when the policies were first implemented in British Columbia. Those policies were drafted and laid out. Do you know from where the New Democratic Party got those policies? It looked at Cominco, part of the free entreprise market, to see how Cominco made deals with the mining industry. The New Democratic Party in British Columbia felt that if the mining industry was prepared to give Cominco that kind of revenue in order to use their mining facilities and their mining land, then it should be prepared to give that to the Province. That is the policy that was laid out. We found out very clearly that it was not working.
The New Democratic Party implemented a new policy and a mine was started up in Kamloops under the new policy. That mine is still operating and we are able-
No, it is not.

They were shut down from a period of time but they are operating. So let us not have any more of the scare tactics that the Conservatives and the Social Credit Government are trying to bring about with regard to industry in Canada.
The Iron Ore Company, Mr. Speaker, gave generous separation allowances to about 300 workers in Schefferville but has completely refused to do anything for the 700 to 800 other employees who have lost their jobs in Sept-Iles where the ore was concentrated. The company has absolutely refused to consider these employees as permanently laid off. Railway workers are also losing their jobs. This is why I say that we cannot zero in on only the mining companies and the Government's activities. We must also look at the municipalities and the people involved.

Our caucus had occasion to meet with a delegation from Faro in the Yukon. The Government has taken action to alleviate some of their problems. They are doing some exploratory work in a small way, taking off some of the overburden, and that has put some people back to work. I want to say how sad I was as I sat on that committee to hear representatives from the Chamber of Commerce, the business sector and the working sector literally destroying their whole background as their community is dying around them. This is all because of the kinds of mining policies and regulations that are laid out and the programs that are followed. As we in this Party have said, it is time we implement an industrial policy for the country that not only looks at the potential in various parts of Canada but also at the mining industry to ensure a long lasting and stable work force in these areas.
I believe the Member from the Conservative Party who spoke earlier indicated that the taxation policies the Government has brought in with regard to taxation on northern benefits for workers in their bunkhouses has created tremendous hardships in the mining sector. I have asked the Minister to include northern benefits in my riding, an area where people live purposely to serve the mining industry.
As I have suggested, the problem is that the Government will not allow these people benefits under the northern benefits tax. I think that is ridiculous. When a young single person leaves his home to work in an outlying area and stays in a bunkhouse, he does not get the same benefits as does a married man. The married man who stays in that bunkhouse is able to show that as his second home, whereas the single fellow, while he may have residence in another area, will still be taxed as much as $23 a day for staying in that facility.
I want to say that these are the kinds of hardships the Government has created. The Minister may laugh, but I want to tell her that those workers are finding it very, very difficult to communicate and to go back and forth. For example, a single man who was charged under the Unemployment Insurance Act paid $1,000 to come out from the North and protect his rights at trial and then go back again. He was found not guilty, but it cost him $1,000 to go back to his home area to protect his legal rights. Those are the kinds of hardships that are experienced by workers in the northern areas. These hardships must be recognized. The planned new taxation on those benefits will create tremendous hardships for people in the mining industry.
We support the Opposition Party's proposal today, Mr. Speaker. I hope that the Government will look seriously at this proposal to set up a committee that will go across the country to meet with the communities, the workers, the mining industry and the Provinces to come up with a solution that will be of benefit to all.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the Hon. Member complained about certain Government investment in railway infrastructure and ports in northeast British Columbia,

May 9, 1983
Supply
indicating that that was probably taking jobs away from Canadians. Does he not believe that the investment in that infrastructure will make it possible to find new mining resource potential in northeast British Columbia and make that new resource possible, or does he think that the investment in that infrastructure is a total waste of time?

No, Mr. Speaker, far from it. We in this Party believe that there is a time for development of the North, but the time is not now. At this time thousands of people are out of work. To build a new community at this time that will compete against one that is already in existence will create a hardship for the existing community. We would much prefer to see that $1 billion allocated to other areas at this time, such as upgrading the railways with firm agreements to ensure that we will be able to supply the market that we have. When the economy recovers and we start to produce, then would be the time to look at that infrastructure.

Do I gather from what the Hon. Member is saying that when we have all sorts of unemployment, investment is bad, that we should not use Government funds to build a future for Canada, to open the roads to new resources? Is that his vision of the country? Is his vision that in bad times we should restrict our activity, not open up new opportunities or new resources but just hone in on present resources? Does he believe that is the way we should go in building this country?

Mr. Speaker I thought I made it very clear that I do not believe that is a time to develop coal fields in another area in competition with existing communities. Three existing communities can supply the market. To put up $1 billion for expansion in order to create a good atmosphere for our competitors to come into the market, where they can buy it cheaper, where it is northeast against southeast and southeast against northeast, is wrong. We do not believe in that kind of financing. It gives competitors in other countries an advantage.

Mr. Speaker, I was rather shocked to hear the exposition of the New Democratic Party's northern development policy. I am pleased that the New Democratic Party did not exist at the time of Confederation or we would still be waiting for a railroad to be built between eastern Canada and British Columbia.
In all seriousness, I do have a question for the Hon. Member. He complained that mines were being closed. An ore body being a wasting asset, that is inevitable with any mine. When you take the first tonne of ore out, the days of that mine are numbered. Is the Hon. Member proposing that we should not open mines because at some point in time they are going to be closed? If that is not the case, how would he solve the problem of dislocations that come about as a result of a mine closure?

In all sincerity, I think the Hon. Member is losing sight of what we are talking about today. We must have diversity for these communities. We must have a plan for a
community that is beginning to phase out its mining facilities. That is the kind of industrial plan that we in this Party are talking about.
We must be able to see the potential of that area. We must not just walk away from it as the Conservatives would. Their big financiers just walk away. They give 50 per cent to the people, tell them to leave and let the community die. We do not believe in that. We believe in an industrial plan that will lay the structures to carry on the community through another phase, contributing to our country in a strong economic way. However, this needs planning, not the greed of developers who take the iron ore out of the ground and walk away with the profits with no concern for the community.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any further questions or comments?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to speak at some length on the mineral sector and detail measures that this Government has taken and is taking to ensure the industry makes its maximum contribution to the Canadian economy and the Canadian people. I am particularly pleased to do so today. This debate is long overdue. It is the first on this subject in this Parliament and it gives me an opportunity to debate with Members of the House the state of the industry and the role of the federal Government.
I would like to reiterate that on Friday of last week I spent the entire day in discussion with the provincial mines Ministers. It may come as a surprise to Members of the Opposition, but five provincial Ministers present paid tribute to the role of the federal Government and how effective we have been, particularly in the last 18 months of the downturn.
The Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) made reference to ore bodies such as Uranium City. I found that an unfortunate reference in many ways because he was defeating his argument. He and the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), who is a very knowledgeable miner, and I say that in a very positive sense, know that an ore body is a finite thing. That ore body declines to a point where it is no longer mineable. This is something that Governments- federal, provincial and municipal-must come to grips with. We have dealt with this over the past year.
It would be healthier if I gave some background as to where we are and where we are going. The Hon. Member is quite right, the mineral industry is one of the basic underpinnings of our economy. Excluding fuels, the value of primary metal production in Canada for 1982 was almost $11 billion. A high proportion of this value is exported, nearly 80 per cent, and is a major earner of foreign exchange. Residents of some 175 single-industry communities depend primarily on minerals for their livelihood. Therefore I share with the Hon. Member his concern that the industry continue in a healthy state. I assure the House that the Government also shares its concern.
May 9, 1983

The industry has witnessed a three-year period of declining world-wide demand for its products, a decline that is unprecedented, at least since the Great Depression. In 1982 the value of Canadian mineral production was down by nearly 18 per cent from 1981, which in itself was marginally below the year prior, 1980.
The cutback in Canadian production was reflected in cutbacks in the mining industry of many other mineral-producing countries as well. The reduction led inevitably to temporary loss of employment for many workers in the industry. Depressed world prices in some cases hastened the closure of marginal mines, leading to what might be termed premature economic exhaustion of the ore body, although physical exhaustion of the mineral had not yet occurred. Therefore there were some permanent lay-offs as well.
This must be said. The facts of the mineral exploration are exceptionally vigorous. That may come as somewhat of a surprise. Investment in new mines and an expansion of existing mines is taking place, in particular for gold, potash and in some cases for base metals as well. Therefore the news is not all bad. Also a cyclic recovery is underway which will lead to the gradual hehiring of laid-off workers.
I mentioned in my preamble that I met with Ministers responsible for mines in the Provinces and the Territories as well and the mood was far from pessimistic. During the course of this debate today, I am sure the House will hear further details of some of the expansions and bright spots that are occurring in Canada.
The federal Government has recognized the recent difficulties of the industry and the impact on those who work in the industry. It has moved resolutely to ameliorate the short-term problems and to lay a firm foundation for future success in the face of continuing change in the world around us.
In the few minutes I have today I intend to demonstrate that the resolution before the House is ill-founded in every specific way. I therefore propose to proceed by addressing briefly each issue mentioned in the resolution and to leave it to other speakers to provide additional information on the Government's programs.
Let us look first at taxation. The Government has not imposed punitive taxation on the mineral sector. The mineral policy discussion paper prepared by my officials, to which the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta referred, showed that while the taxes paid by mining as a percentage of profits increased during the early '70s, the bulk of the taxes went to the Provinces. The federal share of mineral sector taxes actually fell from 46 per cent a share in 1969 to 38 per cent in 1978. I will be very happy to show those figures to the Hon. Member. What is of supreme importance is that in this period the provincial share of taxation grew from 54 per cent to 62 per cent.
I suggest that a parliamentary task force would not solve this problem. I believe the Hon. Member should know that we, through Energy, Mines and Resources and through my Department, have a federal-provincial task force in place
Supply
looking at the tax structure in this country. There has been a very healthy exchange of views and it has resulted in some of the tax measures which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced just a couple of weeks ago. These are tax measures which were welcomed by the industry, and 1 might add by the Provinces.
Moreover, I believe it is important to note that the proportion of profits paid as tax by firms in the mining sector is strictly comparable to that paid by manufacturing and other sectors. Notwithstanding this equitable treatment of the industry as a whole within Canada, the Government has recognized the special contribution and problems of the junior exploration industry and has provided important tax incentives in its most recent budget to permit the easier accumulation of pools of capital and their application to mineral exploration and development. The Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta referred to them briefly; I will expand on them.
The deductibility of earned depletion associated with mine exploration expenditures from any income will encourage increased investment in grassroots mining exploration. And this was done, as I said, as a result of our internal task force, with a great deal of help from some of the professional organizations, the Mining Association of Canada and the Prospectors and Developers' Association, with whom we liaise regularly. This benefit, which will be available to all taxpayers including mining companies, individuals and non-mining firms, will be particularly helpful to junior mining companies in raising funds for exploration, especially through the flow-through shares. I am surprised that we did not receive more support than what was received from the Hon. Member when he mentioned it.
The Minister of Finance also acted to adjust the federal investment tax credit provisions of the Income Tax Act to increase its efficiency and make the credit more equitable. A number of other changes in the budget will not only help to achieve these goals but should also encourage junior mining companies to bring their discoveries into production.
Furthermore, the budget recognized the problems associated with the special characteristics of the mineral industry by providing that non-capital, that is, business losses, will now be allowed a three-year carryback and a seven-year carryforward. This will help juniors to bring their initial mine into production, particularly where start-up losses are incurred in the preproduction period due to interest charges on any debt employed. The extended loss carryovers, of course, will be of great value to the entire mining industry due to its cyclical nature.
Then, to ensure that our mineral industry is treated equitably, not only relative to other Canadian industries but also relative to the mineral sectors in other countries, the Government has announced the launching of a major international comparative study of the tax treatment of the resource industry in Canada and abroad.
I find it rather interesting to note, on a visit to another country just a week ago, that we were held up as a shining example of how a Government has made the best use of the taxation system to develop our resource industry. I might add,
May 9, 1983

Supply
on the subject of tax audits, particularly in British Columbia, that yes, there have been problems which were brought to my attention several months ago; and these problems are now being addressed by my officials and by officials at Revenue Canada. I would like to congratulate prospectors and developers of that area, and also members of the Vancouver Stock Exchange, who were most efficient and courageous in arranging these meetings.
On the subject of northern benefits, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member from Kootenay that those benefits are not being taxed this year. The moratorium is in effect this year. In 1984 they will be phased in at a 25 per cent level and there is a cap. I am sure that this fact is not being conveyed to the general public, especially those affected, and I believe it would be very useful for Hon. Members of this House to know, particularly those who are not truly aware of how these measures are going to be applied and how unfair they were to other people in those parts of the country where isolation benefits existed and how unfair they were to those people who were receiving no benefits at all. It was a subject I discussed at some length with the mines and territorial Ministers, and I might point out to Hon. Members of this House that the territorial Ministers were not in favour of the existing system because of its inequity to the people who live within their boundaries. We are going to pursue the possibility of looking at other measures, not necessarily through the taxation system but other economic measures which will lead to the stable development of those areas. This is something I endorse heartily.
With respect to energy and interest costs, the Canadian mineral sector has indeed been affected in recent years by oil price shocks and by high interest rates, as has virtually industry in every industrialized country. Due to its remote locations, much of the mineral industry is subject to higher transportation charges on fuels laid down at those locations. In addition, the basic price of energy increased dramatically in the 1970s. Rather than being indifferent to these problems, however, the Government has acted over several years to cushion the impact of world energy price increases on the industry and is currently working with the producing Provinces to ensure that Canadian industry enjoys stable energy supplies at equitable prices. Again, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that we have been working very closely with the mineral industry on an energy task force and the work of the industry has been exceptional in reducing the energy costs, specifically of the mining industry.
All industrialized countries have been grappling with elevated interest rates as they struggle to contain inflation. The Government's program of economic management has now brought interest rates to their lowest levels in several years. This relief has already had the effect of reducing excessive debt servicing payments which only a few months ago threatened the very survival of our major mining companies. The industry on the whole, therefore, is looking forward to a slow but steady recovery.
What has happened in the last 18 months? What has this Government done? What is our record on job loss and job creation? It is very good. The Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta says that short-term projects such as Section 38 and NEED are ineffectual. I can tell him that I speak from direct experience. I come from an area where thousands of men and women were laid off. With the use of Section 38 and NEED we came through a very difficult winter very successfully. These people are back to work now. Without these programs, the severity and impact would have been far greater. In fact, if he were to visit my community, my riding, he would find an industry in good health and a community in very good health. That is a record of which I am extremely proud. This Government responded very sensitively and very flexibly by the use of Section 38. We created the NEED Program and, in our recent budget, the Special Recovery Program, which will create a large number of jobs.
Officials of Energy, Mines and Resources have closely monitored the situation and ensured that employees and community groups have been fully informed of the application of available job-creation programs to the mineral sector. As a result of this effort and of co-operation with certain Provinces-and I must say that the Provinces of British Coumbia and Ontario have been particularly flexible and co-operative- the record of use of these programs to relieve distress in mining communities has been outstanding. My officials have prepared an information package to assist the formulation and approval of mineral sector job-creation proposals. With the unanimous consent of the House I would like to table these proposals.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there agreement for the Hon. Minister to table the documents to which she refers?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Thank you. An important feature of the job-creation programs in existence today is that they permit nonproduction work on mining properties, which will have the effect of improving the long-term productivity and cost performance of these operations. We found that to be extremely useful. As Hon. Members are aware, especially those in the critics' position, many, many single-industry towns are just that. It was important to put these people to work in areas where they would be indeed increasing the productivity of the operations. We have been able to do that. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that without these measures and the other vital provisions of Canada's Unemployment Insurance system there is little doubt that the current recession would have been a full-fledged depression.
I would like now to deal with foreign markets and foreign exchange. For many mineral commodities some of Canada's mines and plants are among the world's lowest cost producers. Canada's mining companies have demonstrated their marketing skills over many, many years. They are outstanding. Thus
May 9, 1983

it is no accident that Canada became the world's largest nonfuel mineral exporter.
However, in recent years there has been evidence of a gradual erosion of that position. The explanation lies in structural changes which have taken place in world mineral markets over the past years. The following factors do stand out: procurement policies by resource deficient countries such as France, West Germany, Japan and to some extent the United States have led to offshore mineral investment and preferential trade ties. Optimistic growth scenarios and concessional financing by international institutions have led to excess mineral investment in less developed countries, often with involvement by the host Government. Once in place, such facilities often provide a high proportion of that country's employment and foreign earnings. That was painfully obvious during this last recession.
Now, the Government's response to this situation has been two-fold. First, to ensure that Canada maintains or increases its share of free mineral markets, the Government is determined that Canadian mineral production costs must be held to a minimum by discovery of superior deposits and by use of the best technology and other measures to increase productivity. I am announcing a specific mineral technology program today. I am most pleased to do so; the timing is most advantageous.
Second, the Government is committed to ensuring that international institutional rigidities which discriminate against Canadian mineral exports are reduced. For example, officials of Energy, Mines and Resources have conducted international fact finding missions relating to specific products. A cooperative study has been launched with the Mining Association of Canada to identify cases of non-tariff discriminatory trade policy and subsidized production. Finally, Canadian Government officials are participating in a special resource commodity working group of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade with the goal of eliminating barriers on mineral trade at all stages of processing.
I mentioned a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, that I wished to announce an initiative relating to mining, minerals and metals technology. In the past several months I have reviewed federal mineral R and D and examined proposals to meet the technological requirements and challenges of the 1980s. My review has focused on the Canada Centre of Mineral and Energy Technology known as CANMET. Its activities include policy R and D, which supports federal mineral policies, protection technologies to improve health and safety in the environment, and productivity technology to help improve industrial productivity and competitiveness.
My officials and I have consulted Provinces during this review and their input, complemented by the advice of industry across this country, has made a valuable contribution to this exercise. So today I announce an incremental two-year, $5 million program consisting of several elements to provide increased research and development assistance to the mineral industry in the short term. One of the more significant elements includes New R and D funds for contracts to industry in
Supply
areas such as potash mining, hydrometallurgical and biotechnological processing of ores. We are going to look at foundry process control and computer simulation of process where short-term benefits can be identified.
Another element which is welcomed and done at the suggestion of the industry is making CANMET's special facilities and expertise available to industry at reduced cost where this does not compete with regular commercial services. As the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta is probably aware, most of the work that CANMET has done with industry up to this point has been on a cost recovery basis. Recognizing the cash flow situation of the industry, we are reducing the cost of these services.
I should also like to mention that tomorrow I will be announcing the awarding of a contract to Inco Metals of Sudbury to develop and construct a robot which will perform a variety of difficult and hazardous bar and hammer tasks now carried out manually. The total cost of this project is $778,000.
I note that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, but one thing is clear. I have demonstrated that the Hon. Member's resolution is without merit. Although the problems are real, they are being dealt with by this Government by working very closely with the industry and the Provinces. This Government is committed to the solution of the problems of the industry and has the necessary programs in hand and in development.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend and thank the Minister for going into some considerable detail, as one would expect she would in her role as Minister responsible for mines. I note she has made a number of announcements in her speech today, which is commendable, announcing a package for the use of Members on Government aid programs to assist in the hard hit and depressed areas of the country, a new mining, minerals and metals technology program, and certain initiatives by CANMET. One wonders, Mr. Speaker, if perhaps we should not have Opposition days like this more often because it does appear the Minister gets to work.
When the Minister speaks of new programs and initiatives which were largely conducted by the bureaucracy of her Department, Mr. Speaker, I have to think back to the time of the mineral policy discussion paper which took a year and a half to produce and many, many hundreds of hours of consultation, yet there has been no subsequent action. In fact, that policy paper missed the main mark and the Minister did not respond to my suggestion that it actually missed the main priority high in the minds of all spokesmen for the industry.
I would just quote the President of the Mining Association of Canada who said on April 19 that Canada can wave goodbye to its leading position as an exporter of minerals if it fails to remain competitive with an increasing number of other producing countries. Canada is facing a formidable challenge in world mineral markets from many competitors but particularly from Communist and less developed nations. In fact, Communist countries have grown at twice the rate as Western countries in terms of mineral production.

The question I want to ask the Minister is: Does she not feel that it is high time Members of this House had a chance between Opposition days, which may come every year or two, to sit down and really get their teeth into some of these issues as this motion proposes? She said the proposal for a special parliamentary committee was without substance or foundation, if I remember her words correctly. Does she really believe that? Does she not think that there is a place for Members of Parliament between Opposition days to deal with these very substantive questions bearing on the potential for future economic income and jobs relating to our mineral industry?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I answered the questions very clearly. The mineral policy document to which the Hon. Member referred was the very broad framework from which have flowed the kinds of things I announced today. Surely the Hon. Member must be aware of that.
As to his call again for a special parliamentary committee, I think I dealt with that very clearly. In fact we are dealing with the problems of the mineral industry and we have had a number of task forces in place dealing with the mining community, reports of which are being tabled today. Most of these recommendations from the federal-provincial task force, which included representations from labour and from industry, are in place. The short-term recommendations are in place. The work of this task force will continue over the long term and it will report back to the Minister. Surely it is this kind of co-operation in place now which will result in a healthy industry.
I regret very much that there has been very little discussion in this House about the state of the mineral industry in this country. Certainly that is not due to lack of interest on this side of the House. We have been minding the store. I suggest to my critics-
Why did all of your announcements come today?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: -that they have not been particularly active, nor have they taken a particular interest in the industry.

I was very interested, Mr. Speaker, in the statement of the Minister that there was a special international committee working within the GATT framework on the question of trade in mineral resources. The idea behind this, we were told, was to reduce the barriers to trade in minerals at all stages of processing. This would seem to be a new direction in Government policy, because as far as I understand it the old Government policy was to encourage the upgrading of ores and concentrates within Canada; hence the changes to the Canada Mining Regulations some years ago which prohibited the export of ores and concentrates in unprocessed form without a special permit.
I wonder if we could be told what is the Government's policy. Is it to encourage trade in ores and concentrates in unprocessed form, as it appears to be today, or is to encourage the upgrading of Canadian mineral resources within Canada?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: To be perfectly honest, Mr. Speaker, I am rather shocked that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic would have confused the issue. Of course, the Government is committed to further processing and that is the thrust. The Hon. Member is surely aware that there are many tariff barriers in place which prevent the sale of our minerals further processed. The exact thrust is to see whether, somewhere along the way, over the long term we can reduce these barriers so that we in Canada can process these metals further and find markets for them without the barriers which are in place now. Surely he supports this move.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will allow one short supplementary question as there are several Members seeking to be recognized.

I would like to ask the Minister one further question. It deals with the taxation of northern benefits. Last fall a press release was issued from the Minister's office. Since then there has been nothing on paper. Could we now be told how the Minister plans to implement the taxation of northern benefits? Will it be by way of changes to the Act, to regulations, or a series of remission orders? It is necessary that tax lawyers and tax accountants be able to see the written rules which will apply. When will they become available? All we have to date is a press release.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance will be issuing those regulations. I do not know how much time I have available to me, but I think it would be worth while to explain just how they will be put into effect.
We've got the answers.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: I am not sure that Hon. Members opposite do know, because as of this year the moratorium is in effect. There will be no taxation of-
For next year?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: -northern benefits for this year, 1983. It is only in 1984 that these benefits, which will be kept, will be phased in at a 25 per cent level, the first year.
One hundred per cent the fourth?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: The Minister of Finance will be bringing forward that procedure.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on part of the speech that I made and question the Minister with regard to Ontario Hydro purchasing coal from the States. We have a $1 billion deficit involving trade with the States. First, concerning the environmental aspects, U.S. coal has 7 per cent sulphur and western coal has less than one half of 1 per cent. That has a tremendous impact on acid rain. I would like to stress the possibility of a subsidy for moving western coal east.
It's called the Crow rate.

Reverse Crow.
May 9, 1983
Put coal on the Crow.

What is the Minister's program involving the need for immediate action with regard to Ontario Hydro purchasing Canadian coal? There are 14 million tonnes coming into this country from other countries. Byron Creek is shipping a small amount of western coal to Ontario Hydro. The point I am trying to make is that we have a tremendous opportunity right here in Canada. Is the Minister seriously considering it and, if so, when can we expect an answer?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revel-stoke has put his finger right on the problem. It is transportation cost. He is well aware that the cost of moving western coal to the operations of Ontario Hydro is extremely high. That is one of the reasons the coal association of Canada has been a catalyst in changes to the Crow rate. I want to pay tribute to the mining industry and, more particularly, to the coal association of Canada for recognizing the fact that unless the Crow rate were changed, we would not see this situation change.
Charge everybody more!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: This is why it is important for the Hon. Member and Members of his Party to support those changes-
Forget about the acid rain!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: -if he is to see the movement of western coal coming to eastern Canada.

The Minister said that she felt that people thought northern benefits were unfair. In view of the fact that in the Northwest Territories over 50 per cent of the people employed are employed directly or indirectly by the Government of Canada, and they all receive northern benefits including housing, fuel and transportation assistance, benefits of every nature and kind, why would the Government of Canada pay northern benefits if they were so unfair? There must clearly be a reason for them. What is the Government's policy with respect to northern benefits for its own employees, when this increase in tax will conceivably take place next year, eventually with 100 per cent taxation on these benefits in four years' time?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Mississauga South has put his finger on the problem. It is unfair. Why should federal Government employees be receiving a benefit which is unavailable to some of the people, indeed many of the people, in those northern areas?

So, what are you giving them?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: As one of the Ministers at the Ontario provincial-territorial conference pointed out to me, the fellow working in the garage down the street, who was born in Inuvik and is being paid by the garage operator, is not receiving a single benefit.
What are you giving him?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: There must be a better way to produce and come forward with policies which will be fair to everyone in the North. I suggested to these Ministers that we work on it and come forward with some sort of economic development policy which would make it more attractive for people to live and settle in the North and stay there, but one which would be fair to everyone in the northern territories.
Provide the solution.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: The Hon. Member says "Find the solution". I say yes, let us find a solution.
We'll tell you one.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: I suggest that he come forward with some of his ideas. He might occasionally come forward with a good idea.

The Minister knows that our colleague from Peace River in British Columbia has produced a policy with respect to taxation which would significantly assist. For a long time our Party has been discussing significant tax changes involving taxation of people in the North, to make it equitable. Clearly people in northern Canada, where the cost of groceries is three times what they are in southern Canada, where the cost of heating a house is $300 or $400 a month compared to the cost here in Ottawa, should not be expected to pay the same income tax, dollar for dollar, as people here in this city. That has been the policy of the Government all along. When will the Government come up with something which makes sense? We have made suggestions; when can we have something from the Government?
